cue.topic: Describe a building that you find impressive
bullets: what the building is and where it is
what you do or see when you go there
and explain why you find it so impressive

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the Central Library in my hometown, which I find truly impressive. It stands in the heart of the old quarter, and I first went inside with my classmate Tomasz when we were revising for our final exams. The building dates back to 1912, and it was designed in a grand neoclassical style, with tall stone columns and a magnificent glass dome that floods the main hall with natural light. Stepping through the heavy oak doors for the first time, I was awestruck by the sheer scale of the place. Rows of carved wooden shelves stretch up towards a painted ceiling, and a sweeping marble staircase winds its way to the upper galleries. Despite its age, the interior feels remarkably peaceful, so it is the ideal place to focus. These days I go there nearly every week to study or simply to soak up the atmosphere. What I find most striking is how the architects blended elegance with practicality, since the reading rooms are spacious yet cosy. The library was badly damaged by a fire in the 1990s, but the city spent years bringing it back to its former glory, and that effort says a lot about how much people value it. For me, it is a masterpiece of design and a living piece of history. Whenever I show visitors around, it never fails to take their breath away, and I always feel proud to call it part of my city.

roundingOff.q: Do you think old buildings should be preserved or replaced by new ones?
roundingOff.model: I'd say it depends on the building. Historic landmarks are irreplaceable, so they deserve protection because they give a city its identity. But dilapidated structures that are unsafe should make way for something modern. Ideally, planners find a middle ground by converting old buildings for new uses, such as turning factories into galleries.

questions.q: Why do some cities choose to build very tall skyscrapers?
questions.model: I think it mostly comes down to land and prestige. Where space is scarce, building upwards is the only way to accommodate a growing population, so skyscrapers make practical sense. They also act as status symbols that signal economic success and attract foreign investment. However, there is a downside, because towering blocks can cast long shadows and make streets feel soulless. Personally, I believe cities should balance height with human-scale design, so that residents still feel connected to the neighbourhood around them.

questions.q: To what extent should governments control what buildings look like?
questions.model: To some extent, I think regulation is justified. Planning rules can stop developers from putting up eyesores that spoil the character of a whole district, and safety standards protect residents. Nevertheless, too much control can stifle creativity and push up construction costs. In my view, authorities should set clear limits on height and materials but leave architects free to experiment within them. That way, a city can stay coherent without becoming dull or uniform.

questions.q: Is it better to build new towns or to redevelop existing areas?
questions.model: Generally I favour redeveloping existing areas because the infrastructure, such as roads and sewers, is already in place. Building from scratch eats up farmland and forces people to travel long distances. Admittedly, new towns can be carefully planned around public transport, which avoids the chaos of older districts. Even so, I think regenerating run-down neighbourhoods is more sustainable and gives struggling communities a real boost. Cost is the deciding factor for most governments anyway.

questions.q: Should historic neighbourhoods be protected even if the city needs more housing?
questions.model: It's a difficult balance, but I'd argue that protection should usually win. Once a heritage district is demolished, it can never be rebuilt, and it often draws tourists who support local businesses. Having said that, cities cannot ignore the housing shortage, which pushes rents sky-high. A sensible compromise would be to build upwards on nearby derelict sites instead, so that old streets survive and newcomers still find affordable homes nearby.

questions.q: What might cities look like in fifty years?
questions.model: I imagine they will be far greener and more compact. With climate change looming, architects are already experimenting with buildings covered in plants that absorb carbon, and rooftops that generate solar power. Cars will probably be banned from central areas, leaving pedestrian-friendly streets lined with cycle lanes. Of course, technology could also make cities more intrusive through constant surveillance, so planners must safeguard people's privacy. Overall, I'm cautiously optimistic that urban life will become healthier and more pleasant.

questions.q: How far do green spaces improve life for people in crowded cities?
questions.model: I'd say they make a remarkable difference. Parks provide a refuge from noise and stress, and research suggests that even a short walk among trees can lift your spirits. They also encourage people to exercise and meet neighbours, which strengthens community ties. Furthermore, trees help lower summer temperatures in built-up areas. Of course, a park alone will not solve overcrowding, but it certainly makes dense neighbourhoods far more liveable for families and older residents.
